name: Phoenicia
capital: None; leading cities were Byblos, Sidon and Tyre
summary: A group of sea-trading city-states on the coast of modern Lebanon. The Phoenicians spread the alphabet around the Mediterranean and founded colonies such as Carthage.

location.value: The coast of modern Lebanon and nearby Syria and Israel, with colonies across the Mediterranean.

terrain.value: A narrow coastal strip between the sea and the cedar-covered Lebanon mountains.
terrain.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

climate.value: Mediterranean: hot dry summers and mild wet winters.
climate.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

resources.value: Cedar timber, murex sea snails for purple dye, and glass sand.
resources.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

disasters.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

population.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

urbanisation.value: Byblos, Sidon and Tyre were the leading cities.

disease.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

migration.value: Settlers founded colonies such as Carthage (traditionally 814 BCE), Cádiz and Utica.

economicBase.value: Trade, shipbuilding, navigation, industry and agriculture.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea routes across the Mediterranean and beyond the Strait of Gibraltar.
tradeRoutes.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

moneyAndTax.value: Silver by weight, later coins (from the 5th century BCE).
moneyAndTax.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

inequality.value: Merchant elites and kings above sailors, craftsmen and slaves.
inequality.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

governmentType.value: City-states ruled by kings, with varying degrees of oligarchy.

keyRulers.value: Abishemu I of Byblos (c. 1800 BCE), Hiram I of Tyre (969–936 BCE), Pygmalion of Tyre.

succession.value: Hereditary kings, checked by councils of merchants.
succession.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

institutions.value: Councils of elders and merchants shared power with the kings.
institutions.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

stability.value: Independent cities, often under the control of larger empires.
stability.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between cities such as Tyre and Sidon.
eliteConflict.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

armyAndTech.value: Warships (biremes) that later formed the core of the Persian navy.
armyAndTech.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

majorWars.value: Sieges of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander the Great (332 BCE).
majorWars.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

territoryChange.value: Came under Assyria, Babylon, Persia and the Hellenistic kingdoms; annexed by Rome in 64 BCE.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with Egypt, Israel and Greece; rivals of the Greeks for western trade.
alliancesRivals.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

inventions.value: The earliest verified alphabet, which led to the Greek alphabet; innovations in shipbuilding and navigation.

scienceEducation.value: Navigation by the stars (the Pole Star was called the “Phoenician star”).
scienceEducation.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

openness.value: Traders who carried goods and ideas between Egypt, Mesopotamia and Greece.
openness.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

religion.value: Canaanite religion: Baal, Astarte and Melqart.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Phoenicia (checked 6 Nov 2026); Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

languageWriting.value: Phoenician, a Semitic language; thousands of inscriptions survive.

artsArchitecture.value: Carved ivories, glassware and engraved metal bowls.
artsArchitecture.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

socialStructure.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

sharedIdentity.value: “Phoenicia” is a Greek name; they called themselves by their city or as Canaanites.

neighbours.value: Egypt, Israel, Assyria, Persia and Greece.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Phoenicia (checked 6 Nov 2026); Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

ideasReligions.value: Spread the alphabet throughout the Mediterranean.

colonisation.value: Founded colonies across the Mediterranean, including Carthage.

riseSignals.value: After the Bronze Age collapse (c. 1200 BCE) its cities became leading traders.
riseSignals.source: Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

peakPeriod.value: The 9th century BCE, with Tyre leading.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Phoenicia (checked 6 Nov 2026); Quinn, In Search of the Phoenicians (2018)

declineSignals.value: Declined under the Neo-Assyrian and Achaemenid empires.

outcome.value: Annexed by Rome in 64 BCE; Carthage carried on its culture until 146 BCE.

sources.value: Inscriptions, Greek and Hebrew texts, archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia (“Phoenicia”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Modern scholars debate where Canaanite ends and Phoenician begins.

knownFor.label: The alphabet
knownFor.note: The ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets.

knownFor.label: Tyrian purple
knownFor.note: A costly dye made from murex snails, worn by royalty.

knownFor.label: Bireme warships
knownFor.note: Galleys with two banks of oars.

knownFor.label: Cedars of Lebanon
knownFor.note: Timber exported for ships and temples.
